opus-5.5.text:
I think the perception-action loop is really the dividing line between traditional computer vision and embodied AI.

For a long time, computer vision was essentially a passive discipline. We gave the model an image or a video, and it produced a label, a bounding box, a segmentation mask, or a 3D reconstruction. The output was a description of the world, and the task ended there. Whether that description was actually useful for doing anything was not really part of the evaluation. We measured accuracy on benchmarks, and that was the goal.

Embodied AI changes the question. The agent is no longer an observer; it lives inside the environment. What it perceives determines how it acts, and how it acts changes what it perceives next. If a robot reaches toward a cup, its hand may occlude the cup, the cup may move, and the lighting and viewpoint change. So perception is no longer a one-shot inference problem. It is a continuous process coupled with control and decision-making.

This has several deep implications.

First, **what to perceive is defined by the task**. In classic vision we tried to recover everything: every pixel's label, every object's category. But for manipulation, what matters might be the graspable part of an object, its pose, its articulation, how it will respond to force. My own work on category-level object pose estimation and articulated objects came from exactly this realization. A robot doesn't need to know a mug is "a mug" in the ImageNet sense. It needs to know where the handle is, how it's oriented, and how to interact with it. Perception should serve action.

Second, **errors compound in a loop**. In a static benchmark, a 2% error is just a 2% error. In a closed loop, a small perception error leads to a slightly wrong action, which puts the robot in a state it has never seen, which causes a bigger perception error. That's why robustness and generalization matter far more in embodied settings than leaderboard numbers suggest. And it's also why closed-loop feedback is so powerful: if you continuously re-perceive and correct, you can tolerate imperfect perception at each step.

Third, **action can actively improve perception**. Humans do this all the time. We move our heads to see around obstacles, we pick things up to look at them, we push something to see if it's heavy. Interactive perception means the agent can choose actions that reduce uncertainty. That's something passive vision can never do.

Fourth, it changes **how we think about data**. Internet images and videos gave computer vision its breakthroughs, but they contain almost no action information, no forces, no consequences. For embodied AI, the data has to include the loop: observation, action, and outcome. That's why I believe so strongly in simulation and synthetic data. In simulation we can generate massive amounts of physically grounded perception-action data, with ground truth for everything, and then transfer to the real world. Real-world teleoperation data alone is too expensive and too slow to scale.

So in my view, the transition from computer vision to embodied AI is not just adding a robot arm to a vision model. It's a shift in philosophy: from vision as understanding the world to vision as part of an agent acting in the world. Today's large vision-language-action models are, in a sense, an attempt to learn this entire loop end to end. But I think we still need strong 3D understanding, physical reasoning, and well-designed intermediate representations inside that loop, because that is what gives generalization across objects, scenes, and embodiments.

Ultimately, intelligence emerges from interaction. Perception that never leads to action is incomplete, and action without good perception is blind. Closing that loop is the core problem of embodied AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. I think the perception-action loop is really the dividing line between what computer vision has been for the past decade and what embodied AI needs it to become.

For most of its history, vision was an open-loop problem. You take an image, you produce a label, a box, a segmentation mask, and then you're done. The output never comes back to change the input. ImageNet, COCO, all those benchmarks are built on that assumption. The model is a passive observer looking at a static snapshot of the world, and the world doesn't care what the model says.

Embodiment breaks that completely. Once you put the vision system on a robot, every output becomes an action, and every action changes what you see next. If I move my gripper toward a cup, the cup gets occluded, the lighting changes, the viewpoint shifts. So perception is no longer about getting a single frame right. It's about maintaining a useful understanding of the world while you're continuously perturbing it. That's a fundamentally different objective.

There are a few consequences I find really important. First, errors compound. In a classifier, a wrong prediction is a wrong prediction. In a closed loop, a small perceptual error leads to a slightly wrong action, which puts you in a state your training data never covered, which leads to a bigger error. So the question shifts from "how accurate is my model" to "how does my model behave under its own distribution shift." That's why so much of the work in our lab is about sim-to-real and about representations that are robust to the states the policy itself creates.

Second, action is also a sensing tool. A passive camera can't resolve ambiguity, but an agent can. If you can't tell whether an object is heavy or whether a drawer is stuck, you can push it and find out. So the loop isn't just perception feeding action. Action feeds perception. Active perception, interactive perception, these ideas were around for decades but they only become practical when you actually close the loop with learning.

Third, it changes what a good representation looks like. For recognition, you want representations that are invariant to viewpoint and lighting. For manipulation, you often want the opposite. You need geometry, you need to know where things are in 3D relative to your hand, you need to know how an articulated object will move when you pull on it. That's why I've spent so much time on point clouds, object pose, and articulation, because those are representations that are directly consumable by a controller, not just by a loss function.

So my way of understanding it is that the perception-action loop forces vision to stop being a labeling problem and become a modeling problem. You're building a model of the world that is good enough to act on, and you're evaluated not on a test set but on whether the task gets done. I think that's healthy for the field. It gives us a much more honest benchmark than mean average precision ever did.

r002.rationale: It describes image-based vision as an open-loop task whose output does not change the input or affect what the model sees next.

r003.rationale: It does not compare navigation with manipulation or explain why navigation was a more accessible initial embodied task.

astra-6.text:
I think the perception-action loop changes what we ask a vision system to do. In traditional computer vision, we often give a model an image and ask it to recognize an object or estimate its geometry. In embodied AI, perception is part of an ongoing interaction: what the agent sees informs its action, and that action changes what it sees next.

Imagine a robot trying to pick up a cup. Recognizing the cup is only the beginning. The robot needs to work out where it can grasp it, whether something is blocking the approach, and whether the cup moves as it makes contact. If its view is ambiguous, it can move its camera. If the grasp slips, it needs to perceive that and adjust. So actions both accomplish tasks and provide information.

That means perception has to be evaluated in relation to behavior. A visually detailed representation isn't necessarily useful if it leaves out the properties that matter for acting. Conversely, a relatively simple representation might be enough to support a reliable grasp.

For me, that is the central shift: from interpreting a given observation to continually observing, acting, and correcting. The loop is what connects visual understanding to the consequences of doing something in the physical world.

r003.rationale: It does not compare navigation and manipulation or explain why navigation was a more accessible initial embodied task.

r004.rationale: It describes grasping as an interactive task but does not explain that single-step grasp prediction can remain pattern recognition despite producing a physical action.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the perception-action loop changes what we ask a vision system to do. In traditional computer vision, we often give a model an image and ask it to recognize objects or estimate geometry. In embodied AI, the agent has to use that understanding to act, and its action changes what it observes next. So perception becomes part of a continuous process: observe, act, receive feedback, and update.

Imagine a robot picking up a cup. Recognizing the cup is only the beginning. The robot needs to understand where it can grasp it, move its hand, and use new visual observations to correct errors. If the handle is hidden, it might change its viewpoint. That means action also helps perception—the agent can actively seek the information it needs.

For me, this is a central shift toward embodied AI. We need representations that support decisions and models that can learn from the consequences of those decisions. Recognition accuracy still matters, but we also have to ask whether the system can complete a task and recover when something unexpected happens.
